pages.page_summary: This page defines the scalar (dot) product of two vectors, A and B, as A·B = AB cos θ. It explains the geometric interpretation of the dot product as the product of the magnitude of one vector and the projection of the other. The page derives the component form of the dot product (A·B = Ax Bx + Ay By + Az Bz) and lists its properties, including the commutative and distributive laws. It also provides the dot products of unit vectors (î·î = 1, î·ĵ = 0) and includes a worked example (Example 5.1) to find the angle between two force and displacement vectors.
knowledge_points: The scalar product of two vectors A and B is defined as A·B = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between them.
The dot product is a scalar quantity, even though the individual vectors have direction.
Geometrically, A·B is the product of the magnitude of A and the projection of B onto A (B cos θ), or the product of the magnitude of B and the projection of A onto B (A cos θ).
The scalar product follows the commutative law: A·B = B·A.
The scalar product obeys the distributive law: A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C.
The scalar product is distributive over scalar multiplication: A·(λB) = λ(A·B).
For unit vectors, î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 and î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0.
Given two vectors A = Ax î + Ay ĵ + Az k̂ and B = Bx î + By ĵ + Bz k̂, their scalar product is A·B = Ax Bx + Ay By + Az Bz.
The square of the magnitude of a vector A is A·A = Ax² + Ay² + Az².
The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is zero (A·B = 0).
Example 5.1 demonstrates how to find the angle between two vectors F and d using the formula cos θ = (F·d) / (|F||d|).
